nodes.summary: A list $e_1, \dots, e_k$ of validated edges on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, read newest first, is newest-first acyclic when, for every $i$, the endpoints of $e_i$ are not connected by the later list $e_{i+1}, \dots, e_k$ in the sense of connectivity by a newest-first edge list.
nodes.title: Acyclicity of a newest-first edge list

nodes.summary: A list $e_1, \dots, e_k$ of validated edges on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ is acyclic when, for every $i$, the endpoints of $e_i$ are not connected by the preceding edges $e_1, \dots, e_{i-1}$, in the sense of connectivity by an edge list.
nodes.title: Acyclic edge list

nodes.summary: Connectivity of vertices $u$ and $v$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ by a list of validated edges, read newest first, is defined by recursion on the list. By the empty list, $u$ and $v$ are connected exactly when $u = v$. By a list whose first edge $e$ has source $a$ and target $b$ and whose remaining edges form the list $L$, the vertices $u$ and $v$ are connected when $u$ and $v$ are connected by $L$, or $u$ is connected…
nodes.title: Connectivity by a newest-first edge list

nodes.summary: Vertices $u$ and $v$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ are connected by a list $e_1, \dots, e_k$ of validated edges when they are connected by the reversed list $e_k, \dots, e_1$ in the sense of connectivity by a newest-first edge list.
nodes.title: Connectivity by an edge list

nodes.summary: Given natural numbers $n$ and $i$ and a raw edge with source $s$, target $t$ and weight $w$, decoding at ordinal $i$ returns the validated edge on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with ordinal $i$, source $s$, target $t$ and weight $w$ when $s < n$ and $t < n$, and returns no edge otherwise.
nodes.title: Decoding a raw edge at an ordinal

nodes.summary: For a natural number $n$, an input graph on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ consists of a list of raw edges, kept in input order; the same pair of endpoints may occur on several edges.
nodes.title: Kruskal input graph

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be an input graph on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, give each valid edge with weight $w$ and input ordinal $o$ the key $(w, o)$, and compare keys lexicographically. The graph $G$ has the greedy cut property when the following holds for every way of splitting the valid edges of $G$, sorted by key, into an initial segment, an edge $e$ and a final segment. Let $P$ be the union-find partition obtained by…
nodes.title: Greedy cut property of Kruskal's scan

nodes.summary: The initial forest on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ is the parent forest in which every vertex is its own parent, so every vertex is a root, and whose depth certificate is $0$ at every vertex.
nodes.title: Discrete parent forest

nodes.summary: For an input graph $G$ on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, a list $e_1, \dots, e_k$ of validated edges is an ordered spanning forest of $G$ when it is a spanning forest of $G$ and its keys are nondecreasing: for all $i < j$, the key of $e_i$ is at most the key of $e_j$, where the key of an edge with weight $w$ and input ordinal $o$ is the pair $(w, o)$ and keys are compared lexicographically.
nodes.title: Ordered spanning forest

nodes.summary: For an input graph $G$ on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, a list $F$ of validated edges is a spanning forest of $G$ when every edge of $F$ is a valid edge of $G$, $F$ is acyclic, and $F$ spans $G$: for every valid edge of $G$, its endpoints are connected by $F$.
nodes.title: Spanning forest of an input graph

nodes.summary: For pairs of natural numbers $(w, i)$ and $(w', i')$, $(w, i) \preceq (w', i')$ holds when $w < w'$, or $w = w'$ and $i \le i'$. This is the non-strict lexicographic order on $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$; Kruskal's algorithm applies it to keys (weight, input ordinal).
nodes.title: Lexicographic order on edge keys

nodes.summary: The sorting key of a weighted edge $e$ is the pair $(w(e), i(e)) \in \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ of its weight $w(e)$ and its input ordinal $i(e)$, the zero-based position of $e$ in the original input edge list.
nodes.title: Sorting key of a weighted edge

nodes.summary: For every graph $G$, the edge list returned by Kruskal's algorithm on $G$ is acyclic: each edge in it joins two vertices that are not connected by the edges before it in the list.
nodes.title: Kruskal's output is acyclic

nodes.summary: For every graph $G$ on $n$ vertices, every edge in the list returned by Kruskal's algorithm on $G$ is a valid edge of $G$: an input edge whose two endpoints are both below $n$, carrying its input ordinal.
nodes.title: Kruskal selects only valid input edges

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a graph and let $e_1, \dots, e_m$ be its valid edges sorted lexicographically by key (weight, then input ordinal). For a position $k$, let $P_k$ be the partition of the vertices given by the union-find forest after Kruskal's scan, started from the discrete forest, has processed $e_1, \dots, e_{k-1}$. If the endpoints of $e_k$ lie in different classes of $P_k$, then for every valid edge $c$ of $G$ whose…
nodes.title: Kruskal's greedy cut property

nodes.summary: For every graph $G$, the edge list returned by Kruskal's algorithm on $G$ is a spanning forest of $G$ (its edges are valid edges of $G$, it is acyclic, and it connects the endpoints of every valid edge of $G$), and whenever an edge $e$ comes before an edge $f$ in it, the key (weight, input ordinal) of $e$ is lexicographically at most that of $f$.
nodes.title: Kruskal's output is a sorted spanning forest

nodes.summary: For every graph $G$, the edge list returned by Kruskal's algorithm on $G$ is a spanning forest of $G$: every edge in it is a valid edge of $G$, it is acyclic, and it connects the two endpoints of every valid edge of $G$.
nodes.title: Kruskal's output is a spanning forest

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a graph and let $e_1, \dots, e_m$ be its valid edges sorted lexicographically by key (weight, then input ordinal). For a position $k$, let $P_k$ be the partition of the vertices given by the union-find forest after Kruskal's scan, started from the discrete forest, has processed $e_1, \dots, e_{k-1}$. If the endpoints of $e_k$ lie in different classes of $P_k$, then the weight of $e_k$ is at most the…
nodes.title: Kruskal accepts light edges

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a graph with natural-number edge weights, and let $F$ be any spanning forest of $G$: a list of valid edges of $G$ that is acyclic and connects the endpoints of every valid edge of $G$. Then the total weight of the edge list returned by Kruskal's algorithm on $G$ is at most the total weight of $F$.
nodes.title: Kruskal's algorithm gives a minimum spanning forest

nodes.summary: For every graph $G$, if an edge $e$ comes before an edge $f$ in the list returned by Kruskal's algorithm on $G$, then $e$ has smaller weight than $f$, or the same weight as $f$ and input ordinal at most that of $f$.
nodes.title: Kruskal's output is sorted by key

nodes.summary: For every finite weighted multigraph $G$ on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, given by its list of input edges, and every valid input edge of $G$ (one whose endpoints are both less than $n$), the two endpoints of that edge are connected by the edges that Kruskal's algorithm selects on $G$.
nodes.title: Kruskal's selected edges span the graph

nodes.summary: For a finite weighted multigraph $G$ on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, Kruskal's algorithm starts from the partition of the vertices into singletons and processes the valid input edges of $G$ (those whose endpoints are both less than $n$) in lexicographic order of (weight, input position). An edge whose endpoints lie in different classes of the current partition is accepted and its two classes are merged; an…
nodes.title: Kruskal's algorithm

nodes.summary: For a finite weighted multigraph $G$ on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, the ordered edges of $G$ are its valid input edges (those whose endpoints are both less than $n$), sorted by merge sort in lexicographic order of (weight, input position): by nondecreasing weight, with edges of equal weight in input order.
nodes.title: Valid edges in Kruskal order

nodes.summary: A raw edge is an undirected weighted input edge given by three natural numbers: two endpoints, which are not yet checked to be vertices of the graph, and a weight.
nodes.title: Raw input edge

nodes.summary: Starting from a Kruskal scan state $s$, scanning a list of validated edges $e_1, \dots, e_k$ applies one Kruskal step to each edge in list order: the scan of the empty list returns $s$, and the scan of $e_1, \dots, e_k$ is the scan of $e_2, \dots, e_k$ from the state obtained by processing $e_1$ in $s$.
nodes.title: Scanning a list of edges

nodes.summary: Sorting a list of validated edges is merge sort with the comparison $(w, i) \preceq (w', i')$ if $w < w'$, or $w = w'$ and $i \le i'$, applied to the pairs (weight, input position) of the edges.
nodes.title: Sorting edges by weight and input position

nodes.summary: A list $L$ of validated edges spans a finite weighted multigraph $G$ on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ when, for every valid input edge of $G$ (one whose endpoints are both less than $n$), the two endpoints of that edge are connected using the edges of $L$.
nodes.title: Edge lists spanning a graph

nodes.summary: A state of the Kruskal scan on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ consists of a union-find parent forest on these vertices, which records the current partition, and the list of edges accepted so far, newest first.
nodes.title: Kruskal scan state

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a Kruskal scan state and $e$ a validated edge with endpoints $u$ and $v$. If $u$ and $v$ are equivalent in the union-find forest of $s$, processing $e$ leaves $s$ unchanged. Otherwise $e$ is accepted: the new forest is the union of $u$ and $v$ in the forest of $s$, and $e$ is put at the front of the list of accepted edges.
nodes.title: One Kruskal step

nodes.summary: The total weight of a list of validated edges is the sum of the weights of its entries, each entry counted once, so parallel edges and repeated entries each contribute their weight.
nodes.title: Total weight of a Kruskal edge list

nodes.summary: Given $n$, a starting ordinal $o$ and a list of raw edges $e_0, e_1, \dots, e_{m-1}$, this returns, in input order, the weighted edges on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ obtained from those $e_k$ whose two endpoints are both less than $n$; each keeps the endpoints and weight of $e_k$ and carries the ordinal $o + k$. Edges with an endpoint at least $n$ are omitted, but they still count towards the ordinals of later…
nodes.title: Validating an edge list from a given ordinal

nodes.summary: For a graph $G$ on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ given by its list of raw edges $e_0, e_1, \dots, e_{m-1}$, the valid edges of $G$ are, in input order, the weighted edges obtained from those $e_k$ whose two endpoints are both less than $n$; each keeps the endpoints and weight of $e_k$ and carries its zero-based input ordinal $k$. Edges with an endpoint at least $n$ are omitted.
nodes.title: Valid edges of an input graph

nodes.summary: A weighted edge on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ consists of an ordinal, a natural number recording its zero-based position in the original input list, two endpoints in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, and a natural-number weight.
nodes.title: Weighted edge

can_prove.label: ready to prove
can_prove.meaning: Statement is in Lean and nothing it needs is blocked, so the proof can start.

can_state.label: ready to state
can_state.meaning: Everything its statement uses is in Lean, so the statement can be written in Lean.

conditional.label: conditionally proved
conditional.meaning: Proof compiles, but rests on an open statement without a recorded Lean proof.

fully_proved.label: fully proved
fully_proved.meaning: Proved, and every prerequisite is fully proved too.

inventory_checked.label: inventory checked
inventory_checked.meaning: Module inventory checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

inventory_pending.label: inventory pending
inventory_pending.meaning: Module inventory not yet checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

not_ready.label: not ready
not_ready.meaning: Needs more blueprint work before it can be attempted.

proved.label: proved
proved.meaning: Proof compiles, but something it rests on is not finished.

stated.label: statement formalized
stated.meaning: Statement is in Lean; the proof is not.
